pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 precision extends from words to SYMBOLS and UNITS. Three strands: use the equals sign to mean 'is the same as' (both sides balance) rather than 'the answer comes next'; always include a unit with a measurement ('12 cm', not '12'); and use precise terms for 3-D shapes (edge, vertex, face) and comparisons (greater than, less than). The equals-sign strand is the load-bearing one: Falkner, Levi and Carpenter documented that most primary children read '=' operationally, so a running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 looks fine to them — teaching must confront this directly with true/false and open number sentences and a balance image.
bestPractices: Teach '=' as balance from the start — use true/false sentences (is 7+5=12+3 true?) and open sentences (8+4=□+5) so it means 'the same as', not 'write the answer' (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Insist a measurement answer carries its unit — '12 what?' — because a bare number does not say how much (CCSS: specify units)
Name and touch the parts of 3-D shapes: face (a flat surface), edge (where two faces meet), vertex (a corner point), so words attach to features
State the meaning of the symbols used (=, >, <) and read them aloud in words, so notation carries agreed meaning (CCSS)
Value carefully formulated explanations — have children say the sentence in words and check both sides agree
keyRepresentations: Pan balance / balance scale for the equals sign
3-D shapes with face, edge, vertex labelled and handled
Measurement answers written with units (12 cm, 3 kg)
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' operationally as 'the answer is / and then', writing running chains like 7+5=12+3=15 (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Fills 8+4=□+5 with 12 (the total so far) or 17 (everything added), not 7
Omits units, giving '12' for a length that is 12 cm — treating the unit as optional (CCSS)
Describes 3-D shapes with 2-D or loose words — 'corner' for vertex, 'side' for face, or calls a cube a 'square'

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, extend precision from words to symbols and units across three strands: (1) read '=' relationally as 'is the same as / both sides balance', not operationally as 'the answer comes next'; (2) always attach a unit to a measurement ('12 cm', not '12'); (3) use precise vocabulary for 3-D shapes (face, edge, vertex) and comparisons (greater than, less than). The equals-sign strand is the load-bearing one: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter documented that most primary children read '=' operationally, so a running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 looks correct to them. Confront this directly with true/false sentences, open number sentences, and a balance representation. A pan-balance interaction can make the meaning concrete, but a dialogue partner, a rotatable 3-D model, and screener items each serve distinct purposes and are preserved below.

activities.title: Weigh the sentence: does '=' balance?
feedback: If the child says 7+5=12+3 is fine because they 'did the steps', show the pans: 12 does not weigh the same as 15, so the sentence cannot be true even though each step was computed correctly.
If 8+4=□+5 is filled with 12 (the running total) or 17 (everything added), point back to the pans — the left side already weighs 12, so the right side needs 7 to level, not 12 or 17.
When the child rebalances a false sentence into a true one, confirm that both sides now weigh the same and have them read the whole sentence aloud in words.
activities.rationale: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter found most primary children read '=' operationally and that true/false and open number sentences build the relational 'is the same as' meaning. A live balance representation lets a child see non-equal sides and construct balanced open sentences by direct manipulation. The optional tipping/levelling animation can make the relational meaning concrete; it is an example mechanism, not the only route.
sourceClaims: Most primary children interpret '=' operationally as 'the answer is', so few correctly complete 8+4=□+5 (they give 12 or 17); true/false and open number sentences build the relational 'is the same as' meaning
Proficient students state the meaning of the symbols they choose, using the equal sign consistently and appropriately, and are careful about specifying units of measure
learnerActions: Take a friend's working, 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 = 15, and look only at the middle part: 7 + 5 = 12 + 3.

Using identical cubes (each cube weighs the same), place 7+5 cubes on the left pan and 12+3 cubes on the right pan of a pan balance and observe which way it tips (left holds 12 cubes, right holds 15, so the heavier right pan sinks and the lighter left pan rises — it does not balance).
Say aloud what '=' promises: both sides weigh the same.
Decide whether 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 is true or false, and explain using the balance.
Make both sides the same a different way, e.g. check that 3 + 5 = 6 + 2 (both are 8).
Complete an open sentence like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 by making the pans level, and say what number balances it (7).
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same amount; it is not an arrow pointing to the next answer. A running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 misuses '='. A balance that tips or levels makes this relationship visible.

activities.title: '12 what?' — the unit is part of the answer
feedback: If the child gives a bare '12' and is untroubled by '12 what?', contrast 12 cm with 12 m so the difference in size is obvious.
Confirm when the child spontaneously includes a unit and can explain why '12' alone is ambiguous.
activities.rationale: CCSS MP6 states proficient students are careful about specifying units of measure. An optional 'measuring station that refuses a bare number until a unit is chosen' can make this requirement concrete, but the core aim is that the child states and justifies the unit, not that any particular gating mechanism is used.
sourceClaims: Proficient students state the meaning of the symbols they choose, using the equal sign consistently and appropriately, and are careful about specifying units of measure
learnerActions: Measure an object (e.g. a pencil) and give the measurement.
When you answer '12', state the unit: 12 what? Could it be 12 metres, 12 centimetres?
Compare 12 cm with 12 m aloud and say why the unit changes what the number means.
Write the measurement with its unit (e.g. '12 cm', '3 kg') and read it aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: A bare number does not say how much; the unit is part of the measurement answer and changes its meaning entirely (12 cm vs 12 m).

activities.title: Name and touch the parts of a 3-D shape
feedback: If the child says 'corner' for vertex or 'side' for face, pair the correct term to the feature: edge is where two faces meet, vertex is a corner point, face is a flat surface.
If the child names a solid by one of its faces (e.g. calls a cube a 'square'), distinguish the whole solid from the flat square faces that make it up.
activities.rationale: EEF guidance recommends building precise mathematical vocabulary from informal to formal, attaching words to features through handling and talk. A rotatable on-screen 3-D model and a physical solid each help this spatial strand; a physical solid can be picked up and turned, while a screen model can be rotated and tapped to label — different experiences, neither uniquely necessary. Note this strand is spatial, whereas the equals-sign and units strands are not.
sourceClaims: Precise mathematical vocabulary should be built from informal to formal, with words attached to features (sides, corners) through handling and talk
learnerActions: Handle or rotate a 3-D solid (e.g. a cube-shaped block).
Point to and name each part: a face (a flat surface), an edge (where two faces meet), a vertex (a corner point).
Say which is which when asked to point to a face, an edge, and a vertex on the solid.
Use the precise words: say 'face' rather than 'side', learn 'vertex' as the mathematical name for a corner (corner is the everyday word), and do not call a cube a 'square'.
activities.intendedInsight: 3-D shapes have precise, named parts — face, edge, vertex — and a face is not the same as the 'side' of a flat shape; attaching the word to the felt feature is intended to help the vocabulary take hold.

activities.title: Convince the pedantic listener
feedback: If the child defends a running chain, have them restate what '=' promises and check both sides agree.
Prompt the child to say the sentence in words and confirm both sides are the same before the character accepts it.
activities.rationale: Valuing carefully formulated explanations — saying the sentence in words and checking both sides agree — supports MP6's emphasis on stating the meaning of symbols. A dialogue partner can draw out and repair imprecise statements; it is offered alongside, not instead of, the balance work, since talk may surface reasoning that a scored item does not.
sourceClaims: Proficient students state the meaning of the symbols they choose, using the equal sign consistently and appropriately, and are careful about specifying units of measure
learnerActions: Talk with an in-role character (e.g. a robot or shopkeeper) who reads notation literally and only accepts true, fully specified statements.
When the character asks 'you said 12 — 12 what?', supply the unit.
When the character asks 'is 7 + 5 really the same as 12 + 3?', state whether it is true and why.
Repair any imprecise statement so the literal-minded listener accepts it.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise symbol and unit use is what makes a statement unambiguous to a listener; explaining and repairing out loud may deepen the child's reasoning behind '=' and units.

activities.title: True/false and unit-completion screener
feedback: A wrong true/false verdict or a bare-number answer signals an operational reading of '=' or a dropped unit; follow with the balance task and the 'say it in words' discussion to surface the child's reasoning.
Use correct verdicts cautiously: the sorting items show the error pattern but do not by themselves reveal why the child thinks '=' means 'and then'.
activities.rationale: True/false number sentences and unit-completion items are natural scored checks that can screen the operational-equals error. Such a sorting check identifies the pattern but does not by itself surface the child's reasoning about why '=' means balance; it is positioned as a feeder into the balance and discussion activities.
sourceClaims: Most primary children interpret '=' operationally as 'the answer is', so few correctly complete 8+4=□+5 (they give 12 or 17); true/false and open number sentences build the relational 'is the same as' meaning
learnerActions: Sort number sentences as true or false, including items like 'is 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 true?'.
Complete 'add the unit' items where a bare number must be given its unit.
Flag any sentence that misuses '=' as a running total.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick true/false and unit items can reveal the operational-equals error and the missing-unit habit, signalling who needs the fuller balance and dialogue work.

constraints: The equals-sign strand is the priority: most primary children read '=' operationally, so teaching must directly confront the running-chain error with true/false and open sentences, not assume the relational meaning is obvious.
A true/false or unit-completion sorting check identifies the error pattern but does not itself elicit the child's reasoning or show why '=' means balance; pair it with discussion or balance work.

A labelled static picture or reference card can display finished, labelled examples but cannot let the child balance a sentence, attach a unit, or rotate a shape; use it only as a reference, not as the main learning mechanism.
The spatial 3-D shape strand (face/edge/vertex) benefits from a handled solid or rotatable model; the equals-sign and units strands are not spatial and need the balance and unit-naming work instead.

Physical solids have real thickness and can be picked up; an on-screen 3-D model is a rotatable representation. Both support the vocabulary strand through different experiences; neither is uniquely required. Do not teach 'can be picked up' as the test for a solid — ask instead about the mathematical shape and its named parts.
Recognition/sorting items alone do not elicit independent construction — have the child build balanced open sentences and state units themselves, not only pick from options.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic: 7+5=12 and 12+3=15, so 7+5 (=12) does not equal 12+3 (=15); the chain 7+5=12+3=15 reaches the correct final total 15 but misuses '='. For 8+4=□+5: 8+4=12, so □=12-5=7. The distractors 12 (running total) and 17 (8+4+5) are documented wrong answers shown only as errors to diagnose, never as valid answers. The check 3+5=6+2 is a true sentence (both sides 8). These values are consistent throughout.

Balance-direction check: the original row stated the left pan (holding 12) 'sinks BELOW' the right pan (holding 15). This is physically reversed — the lighter 12-side rises and the heavier 15-side sinks. Activity 1 uses the correct direction; the original wording is recorded as an original-row error, not re-verified.

The source framed a static image as unable to teach and a quiz as unable to surface reasoning; these were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements. A fixed labelled example can still teach as a reference, and scored items can be used during teaching as a screener.

The source links the operational-equals misconception to a prerequisite reteach topic, but that identifier is an internal reference not resolvable here; prerequisite reteaching is noted conceptually only.

The legacy fit rankings and the single preferred-artefact designation were dropped; the distinct pedagogical purposes of the balance, dialogue, 3-D model, and screener are preserved as separate activities rather than collapsed into one preferred format.
The comparison strand (greater than / less than; >, <, =) is retained in the summary but has no dedicated activity; it could be added if a fuller treatment of comparisons is wanted.

probeDeeper: Is 7 + 5 = 12 a true sentence? Is 7 + 5 = 12 + 3? What's the difference?
Can you make both sides the same in a different way, like 3 + 5 = 6 + 2?
You measured the pencil as 12 — 12 what? Could it be 12 metres?
Point to a face, an edge and a vertex on this cube — which is which?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that '=' means the two sides are the same, so 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 is NOT true (12 is not 15), even though the child was correctly doing the steps; the chain misuses '=' as 'and then'. Surfaced for discussion, not marked.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads '=' operationally as 'the answer is / and then', so a running chain 7+5=12+3=15 looks correct
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with true/false and open number sentences and a balance image so '=' means 'the same as'; reteach the meaning of the equal sign.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the sentence is fine, or when given 8+4=□+5 fills 12 (the running total) or 17 (all added)

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the unit, giving '12' for a length that is 12 cm, treating the unit as optional
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the unit is part of the answer — a number alone doesn't say how much; contrast 12 cm with 12 m to show it matters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers bare numbers for measurements and is untroubled when asked '12 what?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes 3-D shapes with 2-D or loose words — 'corner' for vertex, 'side' for face, or calls a cube a 'square'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name and touch each feature — face (flat surface), edge (where two faces meet), vertex (corner point) — pairing the term to the feature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 2-D or everyday words for a solid's parts, or names a solid by one of its faces

responseLevels.gap: Reads '=' as 'the answer is' and accepts running chains, omits units, and uses 2-D or loose words for 3-D shapes.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, treats '=' as a balance (flags 7+5=12+3 as false and completes 8+4=□+5), always attaches units, uses edge/vertex/face precisely, and can say why a symbol or unit must be exact to be understood.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, agrees '=' means 'the same as' and adds a unit when reminded, but still writes running-total chains spontaneously or slips on edge/face/vertex.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child worked out 7 + 5 + 3 by writing: 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 = 15. Look just at the middle part, 7 + 5 = 12 + 3. Is that a true sentence? What does the '=' sign promise about the two sides?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding an operational view of '=' reads left-to-right as a running total and sees nothing wrong; a child with a relational view checks that both sides balance and flags 7+5=12+3 as false. This is the documented Falkner/Levi/Carpenter split, and the running-chain prompt makes the two readings give opposite verdicts.
